posts.title: Sequence changes and ad-hoc bracing: temporary stability still depends on process, not luck
posts.excerpt: CROSS Report 1479 shows how a late change from paired to single beam lifts on a filler-beam bridge introduced lateral-torsional buckling risk under wet concrete. Report 1525 flags the continuing use of undesigned timber bracing on masonry walls. Both point to the same control requirement under BS 5975-1:2024: an active Temporary Works Coordinator, a live register, and independent checking of temporary conditions before work proceeds.
posts.linkedinReady:
Late changes to construction sequence still create temporary stability risks that design teams and site teams can miss until it is almost too late.

CROSS Safety Report 1479 (January 2026) records a near-miss on an approximately 20 m span filler-beam bridge deck. Shortly before the Category II check was complete the contractor altered the planned sequence: instead of lifting steel beams in connected pairs with precast concrete for temporary stability, the beams were to be lifted individually. That change introduced a clear lateral-torsional buckling risk under the weight of wet concrete. Unbraced single beams showed utilisation factors over 200 %. Temporary LTB restraints became necessary.

The issue did not stop there. Weeks later, and only days before the concrete pour, the need for bracing was challenged again. Design and checking were compressed into a short window with limited space left for installation. Independent checking caught the original risk; clear communication and an active Temporary Works Coordinator are what prevent the same situation becoming a collapse.

CROSS Report 1525 (May 2026) highlights a related and still-common gap: ad-hoc timber bracing to masonry walls that has never been designed, calculated or properly overseen. Partially completed masonry is vulnerable to modest wind, impact or construction loads. Improvised props give a false sense of security and have produced serious injuries.

For contractors, site managers and Temporary Works Coordinators:

• Treat any change to construction sequence or method as a potential temporary works design change. Route it through the TWC and the relevant designers before it is implemented on site.
• Confirm temporary stability (including LTB, overturning and progressive collapse) at every stage of the sequence — not only in the permanent works condition.
• Put masonry walls under construction onto the Temporary Works Register. Reject ad-hoc bracing that has no design, no calculated capacity and no competent inspection.
• Keep the Temporary Works Register live. A late sequence change that is not recorded and not checked is a control failure under BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM.
• Independent design checking of temporary conditions remains one of the most effective barriers. Use it.

Educational only — not for construction; subject to the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: CROSS 1479 — sequence change introduces LTB risk on bridge deck
body.p: CROSS Safety Report 1479 (published 13 January 2026) describes a near-miss on an approximately 20 m span filler-beam bridge deck. During the final stages of design, shortly before the Category II check was completed, the contractor altered the intended construction sequence. Instead of lifting steel beams in connected pairs (with precast concrete providing temporary stability), the beams were to be lifted individually. That change introduced a significant temporary stability concern: the risk of lateral-torsional buckling (LTB) of the beams under the weight of wet concrete during construction. Analysis showed unbraced main beams without rotational restraint at the flange ends could experience utilisation factors over 200 %. Temporary LTB restraints were required. The designer offered to prepare the bracing design; the contractor initially preferred its own temporary works team. Approximately three months later, and only about two weeks before the concrete pour, the necessity of the bracing was challenged again. Design and checking were compressed, most deck reinforcement was already fixed, and installation space was restricted. Independent checking had identified the original risk; the subsequent late challenge illustrates how easily temporary stability can be treated as optional once programme pressure rises.

The CROSS Expert Panel highlighted the vulnerability of single beams to lateral-torsional buckling (especially with load reversal during lifting), the need for plan bracing rather than simple cross-bracing alone, and the importance of clear communication of temporary-condition requirements. The role of the Temporary Works Coordinator in clarifying design responsibility at each stage was noted as under-delivered in the reported sequence. Network Rail has since published Engineering Advice Note EAN03/2025 on consideration of temporary conditions, reinforcing the need for explicit coordination between permanent and temporary works.

body.h: CROSS 1525 — ad-hoc bracing of masonry walls
body.p: CROSS Safety Report 1525 (published 13 May 2026) records ongoing concern about the use of improvised timber bracing systems to support masonry walls during construction. These arrangements frequently lack design, calculations or competent oversight. Partially completed masonry walls remain vulnerable to overturning from relatively modest loads such as wind, impact or construction activity. The reporter noted that such improvised systems provide a false sense of security and that the issue is personal: the reporter had previously suffered life-changing injury when a masonry wall collapsed on site. The Expert Panel confirmed that temporary stability of masonry during construction is a well-recognised safety concern and that ad-hoc bracing without formal design should be avoided.

body.h: Practical points for contractors this week
body.p: Any proposed change to construction sequence or method of working should be treated as a potential temporary works design change and routed through the Temporary Works Coordinator and the relevant designers before implementation. Temporary stability — including lateral-torsional buckling, overturning and progressive collapse — must be confirmed at every stage of the sequence, not only in the permanent condition. Masonry walls under construction belong on the Temporary Works Register; improvised bracing without design or calculated capacity should be rejected. The Temporary Works Register must remain live. Independent design checking of temporary conditions remains one of the most effective barriers against late-sequence failures. These measures align with BS 5975-1:2024 management procedures and with the CDM duty to plan, manage and monitor construction work so that it is carried out safely.

CROSS Safety Report 1479 — Temporary stability risk due to construction changes on bridge deck (published 13 January 2026). CROSS Safety Report 1525 — Concerns with temporary bracing of masonry walls during construction (published 13 May 2026). Network Rail B&S Engineering Advice Note EAN03/2025 (consideration of temporary conditions). BS 5975-1:2024 Temporary works — Management procedures for the control of temporary works. HSE temporary works guidance.

posts.title: Props that ignore the existing structure, platforms with no design: the control gap is still process
posts.excerpt: CROSS Report 1539 and recent HSE prosecutions show the same pattern: temporary works items treated in isolation, existing structure capacity left unchecked, and verbal instructions used in place of calculated safe loads and competent oversight. Under BS 5975-1:2024 the Temporary Works Coordinator must own the full load path and the live register — not just the prop or the platform.
posts.linkedinReady:
Temporary works failures are rarely a single design error. More often they are a process gap.

CROSS Safety Report 1539 (May 2026) is a clear example. Heavy-duty props were proposed to support beams and slab while a defective RC column was removed from the base of a multi-storey block of flats. The props themselves could take the force. The existing beams and slabs could not. No evidence was found that the prop designer had checked the existing structure. Opening-up works showed the beams and slab would fail in bending and shear under the redistributed loads. A more complex temporary works system had to be designed before the column could safely be replaced. Without that intervention, a significant part of the building was at risk of collapse.

The same pattern appears in HSE outcomes. At Paxton House (prosecution published June 2026) temporary timber platforms collecting concrete debris had no design and no calculated safe load. An inspection form was completed, but not by a competent Temporary Works Coordinator. Workers had a verbal instruction not to overload the platforms — with no safe load established and no effective monitoring. A drilling operative sustained life-changing injuries when the platform collapsed on top of him.

Industry commentary on recent HSE cases reaches the same conclusion: the root cause is frequently missing process, not exotic engineering. No Temporary Works Coordinator formally appointed and active; no live register; no written procedure that is actually followed; supervision assumed rather than documented.

For contractors, site managers and Temporary Works Coordinators this week:
• When temporary supports transfer load into existing structure, the design brief must require verification of the full load path — beams, slabs, walls, foundations — not just the capacity of the prop or proprietary unit.
• Reject drawings issued “for approval” that caveats the existing structure without demonstrating it has been assessed.
• Treat crash decks, debris platforms and any temporary boarding that carries load as structures on the Temporary Works Register. “Don’t overload it” is not a design.
• Confirm the person signing inspections is competent for the item and that the Temporary Works Coordinator has closed the permit-to-load / hold point before use.
• Keep the Temporary Works Register current. A folder that is never opened, or a register that stops at tender, does not satisfy BS 5975-1:2024 or CDM duties to plan, manage and monitor.

Educational only — not for construction; subject to the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: CROSS 1539 — props that never checked the existing structure
body.p: CROSS Safety Report 1539 (published 14 May 2026) records a near-miss on a multi-storey block of flats. A defective reinforced concrete column at the base was to be replaced with a new steel column. Estimated characteristic load exceeded 1,165 kN; design load around 1,590 kN. Heavy-duty props had already been installed to support beams and slab either side of the column. The prop drawing was status “For Approval” and included a note placing responsibility on the client to confirm the existing structure could safely support additional loads. No evidence was found that the prop designer had checked the existing structure. Opening-up works showed the beams and slabs were insufficient to transfer the loads and would fail in bending and shear. The reporter designed a more complex temporary works system and method statement. Without those additional works, removal of the column would have placed a significant part of the building at risk of collapse. The Expert Panel noted a failure of the temporary works procedure.
